answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: It is a genuine Wilde line from The Picture of Dorian Gray — spoken by the dandy Lord Henry Wotton in Chapter 1 as he needles the painter Basil Hallward for refusing to exhibit Dorian’s portrait. The novel first appeared in Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine in July 1890 and in expanded book form in 1891, and the epigram is confirmed in the full text of both.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine, July 1890; expanded book edition, 1891
Lord Henry Wotton, to Basil Hallward

source.excerpt: It is silly of you, for there is only one thing in the world worse than being talked about, and that is not being talked about. A portrait like this would set you far above all the young men in England, and make the old men quite jealous, if old men are ever capable of any emotion.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.heading: About Oscar Wilde
author.bio: Oscar Fingal O’Flahertie Wills Wilde (1854–1900) was an Irish poet and dramatist celebrated for his glittering wit and epigrammatic paradoxes. The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890/91) was his only novel; his comedies Lady Windermere’s Fan and The Importance of Being Earnest made him the most quotable playwright of the London stage. Many of his sharpest lines — like this one — are voiced by his characters rather than delivered in his own person.

misattribution.heading: Attribution notes
misattribution.intro: This one is genuinely Wilde — but two honest footnotes are worth flagging.

items.who: P. T. Barnum / “any publicity is good publicity”
items.why: The general adage that all publicity is good publicity is often pinned on the showman P. T. Barnum, and people occasionally reach for that name for this line too. But the exact epigram is Wilde’s, from The Picture of Dorian Gray, Chapter 1 ↗; the Barnum saying is a separate, undocumented attribution.

items.who: Wilde speaking in his own person
items.why: The words are spoken by the fictional Lord Henry Wotton, Wilde’s cynical dandy, in dialogue with Basil Hallward ↗ — so it is Wilde’s writing, but delivered as a character’s epigram rather than a personal maxim.

misattribution.truthLine: The credit to Oscar Wilde is correct: the line is his, from The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890/91) ↗, Chapter 1.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: Lord Henry Wotton is Wilde’s mouthpiece for polished cynicism, and this paradox — that obscurity is worse than scandal — captures the novel’s fascination with reputation, surface and being seen. It reads as a joke and a thesis at once.
The line has since become a favourite in public-relations and celebrity culture, quoted as the original defence of “there’s no such thing as bad publicity.”
